checked_proof_steps.checked_conclusion: The Lean score-swap proof derives each ordered-product comparison from the positive count gaps and strict link order, then sums the direct, third-alternative, and unchanged terms to obtain a strictly larger likelihood.
checked_proof_steps.source_step: Claim C.1 is applied to the direct and third-alternative likelihood terms in the score-swap argument. For a lower log-link value u and higher value v, the positive factors are -u and -v; the claim therefore gives the displayed strict inequality even though the raw logarithms themselves are negative.

checked_proof_steps.checked_conclusion: Lean proves the same diminishing-increment inequality for the exact paired log term, completes the winner half, and obtains the loser half by the source-symmetric count-transpose and score-negation route.
checked_proof_steps.source_step: The U/V partition compares cross-pair likelihood increments before and after nonnegative score shifts; concavity of each two-direction log-likelihood term makes the shifted increment no larger, contradicting optimality if V is nonempty.

checked_proof_steps.checked_conclusion: Lean selects an explicit unit fraction 1/n inside the strict base-likelihood neighborhood and constructs the exact common-denominator integer datasets, preserving the source rankings for both counterexamples.
checked_proof_steps.source_step: The source obtains an open positive perturbation neighborhood from continuity and notes that rational frequencies can be scaled by a common denominator to obtain integral comparison counts.

model_conventions.checked_scope: Lemma 2.1 and every later MLE statement that uses a fixed reference; Definitions 4.1 through 6.1 and their theorems depend only on score differences and are invariant under the same shift.
model_conventions.formal_meaning: Lean fixes one reference score to zero. The source proves that adding a common constant on a comparison component leaves every score difference and therefore the likelihood unchanged, so normalized existence and score-difference conclusions are equivalent to the source's shift-invariant formulation.
model_conventions.why_needed: An unconstrained score vector has translation nonuniqueness, while the finite Lean optimization and uniqueness statements use an explicit affine slice. The source's component-shift proof supplies the semantic bridge rather than an added model assumption.

model_conventions.checked_scope: Lemma 2.3 and the uniform compact bounds used in the proofs of Theorems 5.3 and 6.3.
model_conventions.formal_meaning: The positive-count premise in Lemma 2.3 ranges over distinct alternatives. Diagonal counts are definitionally zero in the source pairwise-comparison model, and the proof groups unordered distinct pairs, so a literal diagonal-inclusive reading would make the premise inconsistent.
model_conventions.why_needed: Lean must state the domain of the positivity quantifier explicitly; the distinct-pair restriction recovers the source model and proof rather than weakening a meaningful diagonal obligation.

reviewed_proof_scopes.semantic_scope: Appendices A.1 through A.3: component-shift invariance, compact attainment and the strongly-connected-component necessity argument for Lemma 2.1; the one-neighbor likelihood decomposition and Claim A.1 strict-concavity calculation for Lemma 2.2; and the ordered-score cut argument and reflected negative-coordinate case for the Lemma 2.3 sup-norm bound.

Appendix B: concavity of the finite pairwise log likelihood, strictness along a nonconstant connected-graph edge, failure of strictness under translation of a disconnected component, and the resulting uniqueness equivalence for Lemma 2.4.
Appendix C: the complete score-swap comparison for Theorem 3.2, including Claim C.1 and each direct or third-alternative likelihood term under the Definition 3.1 count inequalities.

Appendix D: the winner-loser comparison after a directed count increase, the U/V score partition, strict baseline-maximizer comparison, and the diminishing-increment consequence of log-concavity used to prove both halves of Theorem 4.2.

Appendix E: the three-alternative Theorem 5.3 dataset, uniform compact MLE bound, base-point reflection and midpoint identity, derivative proof of the strict base ranking, continuity of the unique maximizer, and selection of a positive rational perturbation followed by common-denominator scaling to integer counts.

Appendix F: the two component datasets and their one-neighbor perfect-fit rankings, the pooled three-alternative likelihood, uniform compact MLE bound, base reflection and derivative order, and the positive rational perturbation that yields the finite separability counterexample in Theorem 6.3.
